title: How text flows through a shell pipeline
purpose: See how each command in a pipeline reads the output of the command before it, and why the order of redirections decides where errors go.
sequence_reason: Each stage of the pipeline changes the text, and the next stage depends on that change, so motion shows the data flow better than one static picture.
summary: A seven-line web server log goes through cat access.log | grep 404 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn. grep keeps the five 404 lines, sort puts equal lines together, uniq -c counts each group, and sort -rn puts the largest count first: three errors for /old and two for /logo.png. Then two commands show that Bash processes redirections from left to right, so 2>&1 before or after > out.txt sends the error message to a different place.
explanation: The pipe connects the standard output of one command to the standard input of the next, and Bash processes redirections in the order you write them.

learning_check.question: In cat access.log | grep 404 | sort, what does sort read on its standard input?
learning_check.answer: The lines that grep 404 wrote to its standard output, not the file itself.

scenes.heading: Count the 404 errors in a log
scenes.narration: We count the 404 errors in a small web server log. Seven lines go in at the left.

scenes.heading: The pipe connects two commands
scenes.narration: The pipe symbol connects the output of one command to the input of the next. Here, grep reads what cat writes.

scenes.heading: Each stage changes the text
scenes.narration: Watch the number of lines change at each stage of the pipeline. Cat sends seven lines, grep keeps five, sort groups them, uniq counts two groups, and the last sort puts the largest count first.

scenes.heading: The answer: which pages fail most
scenes.narration: The final output shows the count for each page. Slash old fails three times, and slash logo dot png fails twice.

scenes.heading: Redirection order decides where errors go
scenes.narration: Bash processes redirections from left to right, so their order matters. On the left, ls sends both streams to out.txt. On the right, the error stays on the terminal.
